e.t: Bazluth is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Bazluth” and “Bazlith.” It refers to a person or family name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, once in Ezra 2:52 and once in Nehemiah 7:54. Because no explanatory definition or verse text is available here, its literal sense cannot be stated responsibly. Its role is to identify the named individual or family in these genealogical lists.

This Hebrew word refers to “crystal,” naming a clear, hard mineral substance. It functions as a concrete noun rather than an action or description, identifying a material that can be valued alongside other precious things. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in Job 28:18. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to crystal as a material.

“Prevailed” describes overcoming opposition or continuing with greater strength. This Hebrew verb is used when a person, force, or condition gains the upper hand or remains dominant in a situation. It appears 25 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages describing waters, battle, human strength, and God’s strengthening of his people. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is described as prevailing and what is being overcome.

Gibbar is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Gibbar” in its only Old Testament occurrence. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. The name appears once in the Hebrew corpus, at Ezra 2:20. Because no explicit definition or surrounding verse text is available here, the safest meaning-level explanation is the name itself: “Gibbar.” Its precise significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding account.

This Hebrew word means “fly,” expressing movement through the air. It functions as an action word, describing something that takes flight or moves swiftly overhead. In the Old Testament, it appears four times, in Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Jeremiah. Its repeated rendering as “fly” supports this central sense, while the surrounding verse determines what creature or subject is being described in each occurrence.

This Hebrew word means “judge,” referring to one who exercises judgment. It is a noun used for a human judicial figure rather than for an action or quality. Within the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Samuel 24:15 and Psalm 68:5. Those references establish its limited use, while “judge” identifies the kind of person or role the word names. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It is a Hebrew word found twice in the Old Testament, both times in Isaiah 47:13, so its meaning is concentrated in one passage rather than broadly illustrated across Scripture. Without the surrounding verse text, the safest conclusion is that its precise force should be learned from that passage. It functions as part of the wording there, not as a general theme that can be defined from the reference alone.

This Hebrew verb expresses the idea of “up,” functioning in sentences to describe movement or position in an elevated direction. Its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence, since the word appears in several different Old Testament settings. It occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Exodus through Lamentations. The central idea remains direction or elevation rather than a standalone object or person. Its use in Isaiah 45:2 is connected with other words describing changes to the path and surrounding obstacles.

Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning remains a hook or catching implement.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Jeremiah 36:22–23, keeping its usage focused on this ordinary household object. Its precise role in each sentence depends on the surrounding verse.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times in two verses and is rendered consistently as “Iddo.” The name appears in 1 Chronicles 27:21 and Ezra 10:43. Without the surrounding verse text, those references establish where the name occurs but do not define anything further about the individuals bearing it.

Since this word is preserved as “Jerioth” in the available rendering, its ordinary meaning here is the individual’s name, not a separate descriptive title.

This Hebrew word means “grieved.” In a sentence, it functions as a predicate, describing the condition of a person or group rather than naming an object or place. The word means “cruel,” describing a quality or disposition characterized by cruelty. In the Hebrew Bible, it occurs once, at Proverbs 27:4, so its meaning is represented by this single occurrence and its consistent English rendering. It functions as a description rather than naming a person or place, pointing to conduct or character marked by being cruel. Its precise force in Proverbs 27:4 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “hundred,” expressing a count of one hundred. It is used when Scripture gives numerical quantities, such as ages, totals, groups, or measured amounts. The word appears 583 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that it serves as a normal number word across many kinds of passages. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the number or quantity it identifies there.

It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 23:27. The available English rendering preserves the name as “Mebunnai,” so its ordinary meaning is its personal identification; its particular role in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “meat,” and it functions as a noun naming food. It names a thing rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel 4:12 and 4:21. This Hebrew noun means “barrier,” referring to something that blocks or restricts passage. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Kings 11:6, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical occurrences. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a physical obstruction or boundary that prevents free movement.

This Hebrew word means “corners” and refers to the corner portions of a structure. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Exodus, in descriptions of the tabernacle’s construction. The word functions as a precise structural term, identifying the places where the sides or boards meet at the corners. Its meaning is consistent in both recorded occurrences.

This Hebrew verb means “tell.” It describes making information known to another person, whether by speaking, reporting, or declaring something. The word commonly functions as an action of communicating what is known, rather than naming the information itself. It appears 370 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that telling or reporting is a broad and recurring biblical activity. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being communicated and to whom.

This Hebrew word means “blow.” It describes the action of forcing or sending out air, and in its Old Testament uses it can refer to breath being given or something being driven by moving air. It occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi. Its precise force—whether referring to breathing or another action—depends on the sentence in which it appears.

This Hebrew word means to shut or stop something, bringing its movement or flow to an end. It can describe closing off access, blocking water, or stopping an action. This Hebrew verb means “testify.” It describes the act of giving testimony or formally stating something as a witness. Its use with kings, prophets, and divine instruction shows that testimony may be spoken by people or delivered as a serious declaration. The exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding words and situation.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “Rechab,” a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies named people in the Old Testament. The name appears 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including several occurrences in 2 Samuel and 2 Kings and later occurrences in Jeremiah. Its precise reference depends on the person named in each passage, but its basic function remains the identification of Rechab.

This Hebrew word refers to feeding or shepherding, whether describing the action of providing for a flock or the people who perform that work. It is rendered as “feed” and “shepherds,” showing how the same word can function in relation to tending animals and those who tend them. It occurs 164 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its central idea is established across many passages rather than being limited to one setting.

This Hebrew verb means “set,” describing the act of placing something into its appointed position. In Exodus, it is used for arranging materials in the priestly garments, so the word focuses on deliberate placement rather than merely possessing or observing an object. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Exodus 28. Its precise force in either passage is clarified by the surrounding instructions, but its basic sense is to set something where it belongs.

This Hebrew word means “returning,” naming the act of coming back or turning back. It functions as an expression for the action itself rather than identifying a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 30:15, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains a return or turning back.

Shahazimah is a Hebrew place name, referring to a particular location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in Joshua 19:22. The English rendering preserves the name as “Shahazimah.” Since the available material does not provide a lexical definition or the verse’s surrounding text, the safest meaning is simply the name of that location. Its precise significance in Joshua 19:22 depends on the surrounding passage and the places named with it.

This Hebrew word describes something marked by “corrupt” or “fault”—a condition of wrongdoing, defect, or blame. It is used three times in the Old Testament, all in Daniel, where English renderings present these two related meanings. The word can therefore describe corruption in a person or situation, especially when an examination finds something blameworthy. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “barley,” a grain used as food and as an agricultural product. It is a noun naming the crop or its harvested grain. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 34 times, appearing in accounts involving planting, harvesting, measuring, giving, and receiving grain. References in Exodus, Numbers, Judges, and Ruth show its ordinary place in everyday provision and farming life. The word can also appear in settings connected with death, but its basic meaning remains the grain itself.

This Hebrew word refers to a “quiver,” a container used to carry arrows. It is a concrete noun describing an item associated with hunting equipment. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Genesis 27:3. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning is the container itself rather than the arrows or the act of hunting.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a gemstone identified as “beryl.” It names a stone used in descriptions of precious objects and heavenly or visionary scenes. The word occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages about the priestly breastpiece, the beloved’s appearance, and the wheels seen in Ezekiel’s visions. Its normal function is as a noun naming this particular stone, while the surrounding passage determines its symbolic or descriptive force. It also appears in a creation-related passage in Ezekiel 28:13.

Beera is a personal name, rendered as “Beera.” It identifies an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 7:37. Because the available wording preserves the name rather than giving a descriptive definition, it is best understood as a person’s name, not as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain Beera’s particular place in that passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “Babylonians,” people associated with Babylon. It functions as a group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 4:9. Its basic meaning identifies a people by their connection with Babylon; the surrounding passage is needed to explain the particular role they have in that verse. This word should therefore be understood primarily as a national or regional designation.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “tin,” a material named in descriptions of metals and trade goods. It appears six times in the Old Testament, including passages in Numbers, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Zechariah. In Ezekiel, it is treated as an object that can be present among other materials and involved in exchange. The word therefore identifies a tangible substance rather than an action, person, or quality.
